summary: NASCAR finalized a $7.7 billion, seven-year media rights deal with Fox Sports, NBC, Amazon, and Warner Bros. Discovery, averaging about $1.1 billion annually. Sports Business Journal's Adam Stern says NASCAR diversified to hedge against declining cable subscribers and to deliver more money to unprofitable teams. He warns that more races on cable (TNT) rather than broadcast networks could lower ratings.
one_line: Analysis of NASCAR's $7.7 billion media rights deal, why it was struck, and the ratings risk of shifting races to cable and streaming.
key_facts: NASCAR finalized a $7.7 billion media rights deal with Fox Sports, NBC, Amazon, and Warner Bros. Discovery.
The deal secures seven years of revenue and an average annual revenue of $1.1 billion.
The deal is almost a 40% increase over NASCAR's current media rights deal.
The Cup Series already faced a 5% drop in viewership this year.
Adam Stern of Sports Business Journal discussed the deal on the Dirty Mo Live podcast.
Stern said NASCAR would have loved to stay with Fox Sports and NBC, but that would likely have meant less money.
Stern compared the situation to MLS, which took a big deal with Apple with almost all games behind the Apple TV paywall.
Stern said the cable universe is declining, with subscribers dropping a couple of percentage points every quarter.
NASCAR wanted to spread its eggs in multiple baskets, and Amazon Prime lets it explore streaming.
Teams are saying they need more money and are not profitable currently, which pressured NASCAR to deliver more revenue.
Since the introduction of the Next Gen cars, profitability has become more difficult for Cup Series teams and teams in other competitions.
Warner Bros. Discovery races will be simulcast on MAX streaming and on TNT, which is cable, not a free-to-air channel.
Stern said teams are concerned because races moving off the broadcast network will probably lower ratings.
